729.title: Cyril of Jerusalem's lectures
729.hook: talks to the newly baptized explaining what they had just experienced
729.howItsDone: In the Catholic Church the time after adult baptism at the Easter Vigil is called mystagogy: the newly baptized keep meeting during the Easter season to reflect on the sacraments they have received.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephrem, the deacon who set the faith to music and taught choirs to sing it. Your line was theology you can sing. Which hymn line stayed with you? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

Jerusalem, the days after Easter. A group of people come back to church who were baptized only days ago. Before that night, they had been taught the creed and the stories, but nobody had walked them through what would actually happen to them. They went in, and it happened: words, oil, water, bread. Now they sit down, still a little dazed, and the bishop stands up. In effect he says: you've been through it. Now I'll tell you what it meant. The talks known as Cyril's lectures to the newly baptized are that explanation.
screen: `BAPTIZED A FEW DAYS AGO.` → `NOBODY EXPLAINED IT BEFOREHAND.` → `NOW, WHAT IT MEANT.`

segments.voice: These talks have a name: mystagogy. And the first thing the bishop says explains the order. He had long wanted to speak to them about these mysteries, he says, but seeing persuades more than hearing, so he waited until they had seen for themselves. First the night. Then the words. Then he walks them back through it. Remember, he says, how you stood in the outer hall, facing west, the direction of darkness, and stretched out your hand and renounced Satan. Then you turned around, to the east, toward the light. Remember how you took off your old garment, and were anointed with oil, and led to the pool, and asked whether you believed in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Every gesture had a meaning, and now he gives it to them. Then the altar. He quotes the psalm sung at communion. In the Douay-Rheims it reads: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet." And he gives them a very practical instruction. When you come forward, he says, don't come with your fingers spread. Make your left hand a throne for the right, because the right hand is about to receive a King. Hollow your palm, receive the Body of Christ, and answer Amen. That's mystagogy. The Catechism of the Catholic Church uses the word for teaching that moves from the visible to the invisible, from the sign to the thing it signifies. The water, the oil, the open hand. After, the meaning.
screen: `FIRST THE NIGHT, THEN THE WORDS.` · `TURN FROM THE WEST TO THE EAST.` · `A THRONE FOR THE KING.` · `FROM THE SIGN TO WHAT IT SIGNIFIES.` · then, large: `O TASTE, AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain one sacrament to yourself. Settle, and breathe. Pick one you've received or watched: a baptism, communion, a wedding, an anointing. Walk through what you saw, slowly, one piece at a time. Water. Oil. A ring. Bread in an open hand. For each piece, ask: what is this pointing to? If you're not sure, just notice the question. If you're new to all this, use a ritual you've seen at a wedding or a funeral. The bell holds the time.
Mystagogy. Teaching given after the rite, leading the newly baptized from what they saw to what it means. Today's word.
Your line: after, the meaning. Today, notice one gesture you make without thinking, a sign of the cross, a handshake, a bow, and ask what it says. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

pairs: from the sign to what it signifies

730.title: Martin's cloak (c. 316–397)
730.hook: a soldier cuts his cloak in half for a beggar and dreams of Christ wearing it
730.howItsDone: Catholics honor Martin of Tours as a saint; in parts of Europe his feast is kept with lantern processions and shared food, and some parishes run coat and blanket drives as winter begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyril's lectures and the word mystagogy: first the night, then the words. Your line was after, the meaning. Which gesture did you stop and ask about? Day seven hundred thirty.

A winter so cold, Sulpicius says, that people were dying of it. A young soldier named Martin rides up to the gate of the city of Amiens. At the gate stands a man with no clothes at all, asking the people going in and out for help. They pass him. Martin has already given away what else he had. All that's left is the cloak on his back and the sword at his side. And he looks at the cloak, and then at the sword.
screen: `A WINTER GATE.` → `A MAN WITH NOTHING.` → `A CLOAK AND A SWORD.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Sulpicius Severus, who wrote a life of Martin and says he knew him. Here's what he tells. Martin draws his sword, cuts the cloak in two, gives one half to the man, and wraps himself in what's left. Notice the half. He doesn't hand over the whole thing and ride off a hero. He shares it, and goes on looking a little ridiculous. Sulpicius says some of the bystanders laughed at how he looked. Others were ashamed, because they had more to give and hadn't given it. Then the night. Martin is asleep, and in a dream he sees Christ, wearing the half of the cloak he gave away. He's told to look closely and recognize it. And he hears Christ say to the angels around him, more or less: Martin, who is still only a catechumen, clothed me with this. A catechumen: someone still preparing for baptism. Martin wasn't even baptized yet. Sulpicius ties the dream to words of Jesus in Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Martin, Sulpicius says, didn't grow proud over the dream. He took it as a push, and went to be baptized. So the story has two halves, like the cloak. A man at a gate. And Christ, in the dream, wearing the same piece of cloth. The Catholic Church remembers Martin as a saint, a soldier who later became a monk and a bishop. It started with half a cloak.
screen: `HALF THE CLOAK, CUT WITH A SWORD.` · `SOME LAUGHED, OTHERS WERE ASHAMED.` · `CHRIST WEARING THE HALF.` · `STILL ONLY A CATECHUMEN.` · then, large: `YOU DID IT TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a coat or a blanket. Settle, and breathe. Start with the cold, not the closet. Where near you is someone likely to be outside tonight? A bus stop, a doorway, the steps of a church. Let one place come clear. Then ask what warm thing of yours could reach it: a coat you no longer wear, a spare blanket, a scarf, or the price of one, by way of a shelter, a coat drive or a parish collection. Choose one, and decide when it goes. If you pray, you can remember that person by name, or by the place they stand. The bell holds the time.
Martin's cloak. Half a soldier's cloak, cut with his sword for a freezing man, and worn by Christ in Martin's dream. Today's word.
Your line: half a cloak. Today, give one warm thing away, a coat, a blanket, or the price of one. Half counts. Day seven hundred thirty.

731.title: Ambrose (c. 339–397)
731.hook: the crowd shouts Ambrose for bishop before he's even baptized
731.howItsDone: Catholics honor Ambrose as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and Milan's own liturgical tradition, the Ambrosian rite, still bears his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin's cloak: one half for the man at the gate, one half for Martin. Your line was half a cloak. What warm thing found a new owner? Day seven hundred thirty-one.

The church in Milan is about to turn into a riot. The bishop has died, and the city has to choose a new one. Two parties are packed inside, shouting: those who follow the teaching of Arius, and those who hold to the creed of Nicaea, the same quarrel we met in the Arian question. So the governor of the province comes down himself to keep the peace. He's a trained lawyer and a public official. His name is Ambrose. He stands up and starts talking the room down. And then, over his voice, somebody shouts his name.
screen: `A CHURCH ABOUT TO RIOT.` → `THE GOVERNOR COMES TO KEEP THE PEACE.` → `SOMEBODY SHOUTS HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: The account comes from Paulinus, who served as Ambrose's secretary and wrote his life after his death. Paulinus says that while Ambrose was speaking, a child's voice was heard crying out: Ambrose, bishop! And the whole crowd took it up. Both parties, who agreed on nothing, suddenly agreed on him. Here's the catch. Ambrose was not a priest. He wasn't even baptized. He was a catechumen, still preparing for baptism, a public official with a career. So he tried to get out of it. Paulinus lists the attempts, and some are almost comic. Ambrose tried acting harsh in court, to seem unfit. He tried slipping out of the city by night, heading for another town, and, Paulinus says, wandered all night and found himself at the gate of Milan in the morning. He hid at a friend's country estate, and the friend gave him up. In the end he said yes. He was baptized, and days later made bishop. Later, Ambrose wrote about it himself, in a book on the duties of the clergy. He says he was carried off from the judge's bench and the robes of office into the priesthood, and so he began to teach before he had learned. He had to learn and teach at the same time. A bishop, putting that in writing. He wasn't ready, and he said so, and he took the job anyway, learning as he went. Chosen before ready.
screen: `A CHILD'S VOICE: AMBROSE, BISHOP!` · `HE TRIES TO GET OUT OF IT.` · `BAPTIZED, THEN MADE BISHOP.` · `TEACHING BEFORE LEARNING.` · then, large: `CHOSEN BEFORE READY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept a task you feel unready for. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing that's been put in front of you, or that you keep stepping around because you don't feel qualified. A role at work. Looking after a parent. Leading something small. Hold it, and notice the reasons you've been giving for saying no. Then picture the first small step, the one you could take this week while you learn. If you pray, you can ask for help with it. The bell holds the time.
Ambrose. The governor in Milan whom a crowd made bishop before he was baptized, and who said he had to learn and teach at the same time. Today's word.
Your line: chosen before ready. Today, say yes to one thing you feel not quite ready for, and learn while you do it. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

732.title: Ambrose and the emperor
732.hook: after a massacre, Ambrose makes the emperor do public penance
732.howItsDone: Catholics confess serious sin in the sacrament of penance, also called reconciliation; public penance like the emperor's belongs to the early Church, and today the sacrament is ordinarily private, between penitent and priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose, made bishop by a shouting crowd before he was even baptized. Your line was chosen before ready. What did you say yes to? Day seven hundred thirty-two.

A letter, written by hand, meant for one reader. The reader is the emperor Theodosius, a Christian, and a man who comes to church in Milan. The writer is the bishop of Milan, Ambrose. Something terrible has happened in the city of Thessalonica. After a riot there, the emperor's soldiers turned on the people of the city and killed them. The emperor is expected at Mass as usual. And the bishop has to decide what to say to the emperor.
screen: `A LETTER FOR ONE READER.` → `A MASSACRE IN THESSALONICA.` → `THE EMPEROR EXPECTS MASS AS USUAL.`

segments.voice: Ambrose's letter is quieter than the legend. He doesn't denounce the emperor from the pulpit. He writes privately, and he writes as a pastor. He grieves over Thessalonica. He tells Theodosius plainly that he dare not offer the sacrifice of the Mass if the emperor intends to be there, not with this on his hands. And he points him to someone the emperor would know from scripture: King David. After David sent a man to his death, the prophet Nathan confronted him, and David didn't argue. In the Douay-Rheims: "And David said to Nathan: I have sinned against the Lord." Ambrose's message, more or less: a king did this before you. You can do it too. And Theodosius did. Ambrose describes it later, in the sermon he preached at the emperor's funeral. The emperor, he says, laid aside the signs of his royal rank, and wept for his sin openly in church, and asked for pardon. Public penance, done by an emperor. Here's where the story grows. A later historian, Theodoret, tells a more dramatic version: Ambrose meets the emperor at the church door and blocks his way in front of everyone. Ambrose's own letter is private and patient. Both versions agree on the ending, though. The emperor stood among sinners and asked for mercy. Even the emperor.
screen: `A PRIVATE LETTER, NOT A PUBLIC FIGHT.` · `DAVID: I HAVE SINNED.` · `THE EMPEROR LAYS ASIDE HIS RANK.` · `THE STORY GROWS IN THE RETELLING.` · then, large: `EVEN THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak truth to someone powerful. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone with more power than you who needs to hear something true: a manager, an official, a landlord, someone older in the family. Shape the one sentence you'd say. Take the anger out of it, and keep the truth in it. Then notice Ambrose's way: privately first, with respect, leaving them room to change. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
paenitentia. Latin for penance, what Ambrose asked of Theodosius after the massacre at Thessalonica, before the emperor could return to Mass. Today's word.
Your line: even the emperor. Today, say one true thing to someone above you, privately and with respect. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

733.title: Monica's tears (Confessions 3)
733.hook: a mother prays for years for her son; a bishop tells her a son of such tears can't be lost
733.howItsDone: Catholics honor Monica as a saint and some ask her prayers for children who have drifted from the faith; her feast falls the day before her son Augustine's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose and the emperor, and his paenitentia: a private letter, King David's words, and an emperor who laid aside his rank. Your line was even the emperor. What true thing did you say? Day seven hundred thirty-three.

Augustine wrote his Confessions talking to God, not to us. We're overhearing. And in the third book he remembers his mother, crying. He's a young man, brilliant, restless, and he has joined a religious movement called the Manichees, whose teaching he later left behind. His mother, Monica, is a Christian, and she weeps over him. He says she wept for him more than mothers weep over a child's dead body. He's writing this long afterward, and he sets her tears down in a book addressed to God.
screen: `A BOOK WRITTEN TO GOD.` → `A SON GONE ANOTHER WAY.` → `A MOTHER WHO WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Augustine tells two moments. First, a dream. Monica dreams she's standing on a wooden ruler, grieving, and a young man, bright and smiling, comes up and asks why she's sad. She says she's mourning her son's ruin. He tells her to look: where she is, there her son is too. She looks, and sees Augustine standing beside her on the same ruler. When she tells him, Augustine tries to twist it. Maybe it means she'll come round to where he is. She answers straight away: no. It didn't say where he is, you are. It said where you are, he is. Augustine admits that her quick answer moved him more than the dream did. Second, a bishop. Augustine doesn't name him. Monica begs this bishop to talk with her son and argue him out of his errors. The bishop refuses. The young man is too pleased with his new ideas, he says. Let him alone. Only pray for him. He'll find out by reading. The bishop even tells her he went down that same road as a boy, and found his own way out. But Monica keeps pressing, and crying. And finally, a little annoyed, the bishop says the line Augustine wrote down. Go your way, he tells her: it cannot be that the son of these tears should be lost. Augustine says she took it as if it had sounded from heaven. Notice what the bishop didn't do. He didn't argue with the son. He sent the mother back to her prayers.
screen: `A DREAM OF A WOODEN RULER.` · `WHERE YOU ARE, THERE HE IS.` · `LET HIM ALONE. ONLY PRAY.` · `THE SON OF THESE TEARS.` · then, large: `IT CANNOT BE THAT HE SHOULD BE LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who's far away. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind who feels far from you right now. Far in miles, or far in some other way: gone quiet, gone another direction. Don't argue with them in your head. Just hold them. Say their name. If you pray, you can place them before God the way Monica did. If you don't, keep them in mind, warmly, without fixing anything. The bell holds the time.
Monica's tears. A mother's prayers for her son Augustine, and a bishop's promise that the son of such tears could not be lost. Today's word.
Your line: the son of these tears. Today, send one kind word to someone far away, with no argument attached. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

734.title: The pears (Confessions 2)
734.hook: young Augustine steals pears he doesn't want, just for the thrill
734.howItsDone: Catholics prepare for confession with an examination of conscience, looking back over what they have done and why; Augustine's Confessions is read as an example of that kind of honest look.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Monica's tears, and a bishop who told her the son of such tears could not be lost. Your line was the son of these tears. Who did you hold in mind? Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A pear tree, next to a vineyard. Loaded with fruit. And the pears, Augustine tells us, weren't even good: nothing special to look at, nothing special to eat. We step back a book now, to Book Two of the Confessions, when he's still a boy at home. Late one night, after hanging around the streets, he and a gang of friends go to that tree. They shake it. They haul off armloads of pears. They aren't hungry. They don't want pears. Long afterward, as he writes, this small theft is still bothering him.
screen: `A PEAR TREE BY A VINEYARD.` → `THE PEARS WEREN'T EVEN GOOD.` → `A GANG, LATE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's what they did with the pears. They ate a few, Augustine says, and threw the rest to the pigs. He had better pears at home. So why? That's the whole question of the passage, and he won't let it go. He says the only pleasure in it was that it wasn't allowed. He loved, he says, not the pears, but the wrong itself. Then he goes looking for a motive the way a detective would. People who do terrible things, he says, usually want something: another man's wife, his land, money to live on, revenge. Even a cruel man has a reason. He can't find his. Then he finds one piece. He would not have done it alone. Alone, he says, it would have been no fun at all. It was the laughing together, the dare, the being in on it. He calls it a friendship that was no friend at all. Some readers hear an echo of another garden here, the tree in Genesis, fruit taken because it was forbidden. The loads were heavy, he says, but the stakes were nothing. Pears nobody wanted. Pig food. That's why it works. A big crime has big reasons. A pointless wrong shows the heart with nothing else in the way. And notice the tone. No list of punishments, no big drama. He's asking, in front of God, a question that's easy to skip: why did I do it?
screen: `NOT HUNGRY, NOT EVEN GOOD PEARS.` · `HE LOVED THE WRONG ITSELF.` · `ALONE, HE WOULDN'T HAVE DONE IT.` · `A SMALL WRONG SHOWS THE HEART.` · then, large: `WHY DID I DO IT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look honestly at a pointless wrong. Settle, and breathe. Not your worst moment. A small one, with no good reason behind it. A cruel joke. Something broken for fun. A rumor passed on because it was juicy. Let it come up. Then ask Augustine's question, quietly: why did I do it? Who was I with? What did I want? Don't punish yourself. Just look. If you pray, you can name it to God, the way Augustine did. The bell holds the time.
The pears. A small theft from Augustine's boyhood, pears he didn't want, taken with friends for the thrill of the forbidden. Today's word.
Your line: why did I do it. Today, when you catch yourself doing something small and pointless, stop and ask the question. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

735.title: Milan (Confessions 5–6)
735.hook: Augustine goes to hear Ambrose's style and stays for the substance
735.howItsDone: At Mass the homily follows the Gospel, and the priest or deacon explains the readings; Catholics who want more may join a Bible study or read with the help of the Church's commentaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pears: a theft with no reason but the forbidden and the friends. Your line was why did I do it. What small thing did you catch yourself at? Day seven hundred thirty-five.

A job offer. The city of Milan needs a teacher of public speaking, and Augustine gets the post. He's a professional now: he teaches young men how to persuade a room. He arrives in Milan and, as part of settling in, goes to meet the bishop. It's Ambrose, the governor the crowd made bishop, the one who wrote to the emperor. Augustine has heard Ambrose is a superb speaker. So when Ambrose preaches, he goes to church. Not to pray. To review the performance.
screen: `A NEW JOB IN MILAN.` → `A PROFESSIONAL PERSUADER.` → `HE GOES TO REVIEW THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: Augustine tells it in Books Five and Six of the Confessions. First, the welcome. He says Ambrose received him like a father, and Augustine began to love him, not yet as a teacher of truth, he admits, just as a man who was kind to him. Then the sermons. Augustine sits there like a critic. Is the bishop as good as his reputation? He listens closely to the words and doesn't care about the content. He even enjoys the sweetness of the speaking. And then something happens he didn't plan. While he was opening his ears to how well Ambrose spoke, he says, how truly he spoke came in along with it, little by little. He couldn't separate the two. He came for the style, and the substance got in. One thing that got in was a way of reading the Old Testament. Augustine had found some of its stories crude. Ambrose kept repeating a line from Saint Paul. In the Douay-Rheims: "the letter killeth, but the spirit quickeneth." Read for the spirit, and the hard passages opened up. And one more picture from Milan: Ambrose reading. His eyes moved over the page, his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were still. Augustine and his friends would come in, find him reading silently, sit a while without disturbing him, and leave. He wanted to talk to the bishop and couldn't get the time. He got the sermons instead.

Maybe their style dazzles you, or maybe it grates on you. Set the style aside for a minute. What are they actually saying? Is any of it true? Take one thing they said lately and say it back to yourself in plain, flat words, stripped of the delivery. The bell holds the time.
